title: Unbounded address collection retrieval without pagination
description: The service exposes a collection read that always requests the entire `/api/Addresss` resource and provides no pagination, limit, cursor, or filtering controls. A caller outside this file can invoke `get()`, causing the backend to return an unbounded address collection and causing memory, bandwidth, serialization, and browser-processing costs to grow with the number of records. If the endpoint is reachable by a low-privilege or publicly accessible user, repeated requests can be used for resource exhaustion. Any infrastructure-level limits or backend pagination are not visible in this file.

The method constructs a GET request to the collection endpoint using only the configured host and resource path; no pagination or result-size constraint is added.
`HttpClient.get()` sends the unbounded collection request to `/api/Addresss`, allowing the server response and client-side mapping to scale with the entire address dataset.

title: Path traversal permits reading arbitrary YAML files
description: `loadStaticData` accepts a caller-controlled file identifier and concatenates it into a filesystem path without constraining it to the intended `data/static` directory. `path.resolve` normalizes traversal sequences but does not enforce that the result remains beneath the base directory. A caller can supply values such as `../../config/secrets` and cause the application to read an attacker-selected existing `.yml` file outside the static-data directory. This is an unauthorized file-resource lookup and unsafe file handling; the caller/route is outside this file.

trace.description: Exported function `loadStaticData(file)` receives the file identifier from a caller outside this file; no trust boundary or authorization check is present here.

The caller-controlled `file` value is directly concatenated into the filesystem path before resolution. No basename validation, allow-list, or post-resolution directory-boundary check prevents `../` traversal.
The resolved path is passed to `readFile`, allowing reads of existing `.yml` files outside `./data/static` and returning their contents to the caller.

title: Caller-controlled path is written to logs without log-safe encoding
description: On a failed read, the resolved path incorporates the caller-controlled `file` value and is concatenated into a log message. If an attacker can reach this loader with a value containing newline/control characters, they may forge additional log lines or corrupt log parsing. Whether the imported logger safely encodes messages is not visible in this file, so exploitability depends on logger output behavior.

The input is incorporated into `filePath` without rejecting newline or other log-control characters.
When the read fails, the resulting caller-influenced path is concatenated into an error message passed to `logger.error`; logger escaping/structured encoding is not established here.

title: Unbounded chat request and streamed response consumption
description: The chat client accepts an unrestricted messages array from callers outside this file and forwards it wholesale in an HTTP request. It also accumulates every streamed response chunk in an in-memory array until the stream terminates, with no request-size, response-size, chunk-count, timeout, or cancellation limit. A caller can submit an extremely large prompt or induce a very large/long-running response, causing excessive browser memory usage and potentially expensive backend/LLM consumption. Repeated invocations can amplify the impact if no external throttling exists.

trace.description: The exported streamMessages method receives the messages array from a caller outside this file; there is no visible bound on the number of messages or the size of their content.
The complete messages array is placed directly into the POST body sent to the chat endpoint, without a client-side size limit, truncation, request timeout, or cancellation mechanism.
A chunks array is created with no capacity or total-response limit and remains associated with the active stream until completion.
Each received model delta is appended to the in-memory chunks array; an attacker-controlled or runaway stream can therefore grow client memory without a chunk or byte cap.

title: Unbounded challenge-list queries
description: The exported `find` method accepts arbitrary caller-supplied query parameters and forwards them directly to the Challenges collection endpoint. It does not impose pagination, a maximum page size, or any other result bound. A caller can request an excessively large result set (for example, by supplying a large `limit`/`pageSize` parameter if honored by the API), causing the server and browser to allocate and process an unnecessarily large response. The server may provide independent safeguards, but none are established in this file.

title: Caller-controlled basket ID used for cross-user basket mutation
description: The service accepts a caller-supplied basket identifier and uses it to read and mutate basket data without any client-side ownership or authorization check. The merge path also places that identifier directly into the BasketId property sent to the create endpoint. If the backend does not independently enforce that the authenticated user owns the target basket and its items, a user can substitute another user's basket ID and add or modify items in that basket. The same flow exposes caller control over the basket-association property, creating a broken object-property authorization risk.

The supplied targetBasketId is used to retrieve the target basket, with no ownership check between the lookup and subsequent mutation logic.
For each guest item, the service either uses an existing server-returned BasketItem ID or constructs a new request containing BasketId: targetBasketId and the client-controlled quantity.

The service sends PUT and POST mutations for the selected basket/item IDs. No per-resource authorization or explicit allow-list for the basket association is enforced before these requests are issued.

title: Unbounded guest-basket merge launches concurrent mutation requests
description: A user-controlled sessionStorage array can contain an arbitrary number of valid basket items, and the service creates one HTTP mutation per unique product. It then passes the entire request array to forkJoin, which subscribes to all requests concurrently. There is no item-count cap, batching, concurrency limit, or rate control in this flow. An attacker can populate the guest basket up to the browser storage quota and trigger a burst of requests, consuming browser, network, and backend resources.

Guest items are read from sessionStorage and reduced into a map without any maximum item count or total-entry limit.
Every distinct guest product becomes a separate HTTP request; there is no cap on mergeRequests and no concurrency throttling.
forkJoin subscribes to the complete unbounded request array at once, allowing a storage-quota-sized guest basket to generate a large concurrent request burst.

title: Unbounded client-controlled basket quantities are submitted during merge
description: Guest basket quantities originate in attacker-controlled sessionStorage and are only checked for being finite and at least one. There is no upper bound or business-rule validation. The values are summed and sent directly to basket-item update/create APIs. A user can therefore submit extremely large quantities, potentially causing oversized calculations, integer/stock-limit inconsistencies, excessive downstream processing, or economic manipulation if the server relies on these values instead of revalidating them.

Quantity is converted to a number and accepted when finite and at least one, but no maximum quantity or maximum aggregate quantity is enforced.
Quantities from duplicate products are added together without an upper bound, allowing aggregate values to grow beyond normal business limits.
The resulting unbounded quantity is sent directly in PUT or POST basket mutations, leaving the server-side operation to handle potentially extreme values.

title: Unbounded retrieval of all hints
description: The service exposes a collection operation that retrieves the entire hints dataset in one request. `getAll()` has no pagination, result-size limit, or other client-side bound, and directly returns the server response data. If the `/api/Hints/` collection can grow substantially and the endpoint is reachable by an attacker or low-privilege user, repeated requests can force the server and client to allocate and transfer an unbounded number of records, causing excessive memory, bandwidth, and processing consumption. Server-side pagination or rate limiting cannot be confirmed from this file, so confidence is moderate-low.

title: Unbounded feedback request body forwarded to API
description: The public service method accepts an unconstrained `any` value and forwards it as the entire request body. A caller outside this file can invoke `save` with an extremely large or deeply nested object, causing the browser to allocate and serialize a large payload and forcing the `/api/Feedbacks/` endpoint to consume request bandwidth, parsing memory, and processing resources. No client-side size or complexity bound is enforced here; server-side request limits cannot be confirmed from this file.

The unbounded body reaches `HttpClient.post` for `/api/Feedbacks/`, where oversized or highly complex input can consume client and server request-processing resources.

title: Unbounded conversation storage permits client-side resource exhaustion
description: The service accepts an arbitrarily large conversation object from callers outside this file and serializes the complete accumulated conversation list into browser localStorage without any size, count, or field-length limits. An attacker or user who can cause large messages/conversation objects to be saved can exhaust the browser's localStorage quota, causing setItem to throw and potentially disabling conversation persistence and any caller that does not handle the exception. Each save also reads and parses the entire unbounded collection before rewriting it, increasing memory and CPU consumption as the collection grows.

Every save loads the entire existing conversation collection, so the amount of data processed grows with all previously stored conversations.
The supplied conversation is appended or replaces an existing entry without checking the number of conversations, message lengths, serialized size, or remaining storage capacity.

The complete unbounded collection is JSON serialized and written to localStorage. Large inputs can consume the browser storage quota and cause setItem to fail, while repeated full serialization and parsing consumes increasing client resources.

title: Malformed localStorage data can disable conversation storage
description: Persisted localStorage content is treated as valid JSON with no error handling. Any same-origin actor or local user able to modify the browser storage can place malformed JSON under the fixed key; subsequent reads then throw from JSON.parse, preventing getAll and operations such as save and delete from completing. This creates a client-side availability failure for the conversation feature.

The service retrieves the raw value associated with a predictable, fixed localStorage key and performs no integrity marker, schema validation, or recovery handling.
The raw browser-controlled string is deserialized directly without a try/catch or fallback for malformed content.

title: Unbounded order-history retrieval
description: The exported `getAll()` method requests the entire order collection through `/rest/order-history/orders` without supplying a page number, page size, or other bound. If the backend returns the complete collection, an authenticated caller can repeatedly invoke this method and force the server, network, and browser to transfer and materialize an arbitrarily large order-history response, causing elevated memory and bandwidth consumption or service degradation. Server-side pagination or an enforced maximum result size is not visible in this file.

title: Unbounded local backup size causes browser resource exhaustion
description: The restore operation reads the entire caller-supplied File into memory and then parses the complete contents as one JSON document without any size limit. A caller outside this file can pass an extremely large or highly nested backup file; `File.text()` allocates the full content and `JSON.parse()` creates another in-memory representation, potentially exhausting browser memory or causing significant CPU usage and UI unavailability. The error handler only handles parsing failure after the resource-intensive read/parse has already occurred.

title: Unbounded photo upload forwarded without resource limits
description: The photo upload path forwards an arbitrary caller-provided File directly in a multipart request without any client-side size, count, or type bounds. A caller of `addMemory` (outside this file) can supply a very large file, causing the browser and upload endpoint to allocate and transfer excessive data; repeated calls can amplify bandwidth, memory, storage, and processing consumption. title: Client-controlled review author enables authorship spoofing
description: The review creation method accepts `author` from its caller and forwards it directly in the PUT request. Review authorship is an identity-sensitive property that should be derived from the authenticated session on the server, not trusted from client input. An attacker who can invoke this service or modify the request can submit a review attributed to another user or an arbitrary identity if the backend accepts the field. The TypeScript type is not an authorization control and does not protect the HTTP API at runtime.

title: Unbounded quantity collection retrieval

title: Caller-controlled security-question lookup enables account enumeration
description: The service exposes a security-question lookup that accepts an arbitrary caller-supplied email address and sends it directly to the security-question endpoint. No authorization or proof of account ownership is enforced in this service. If the endpoint is reachable without an already authenticated session, an attacker can enumerate users and retrieve their security questions, reducing the protection of the account-recovery workflow and assisting targeted guessing attacks. The caller and server-side authorization behavior are outside this file, so reachability and exploitability depend on those controls.

title: Password-change credentials exposed in a GET query string
description: The password-change request places the current password, new password, and repeated password directly in the URL query string and uses GET. URL query values can be captured by browser history, reverse-proxy/web-server logs, monitoring systems, analytics, and referrer propagation. The test asserts this behavior explicitly, indicating that the UserService implementation sends credential material this way. An attacker who obtains such URL data may recover plaintext passwords or password-reset material.

title: OAuth access token exposed in request URL
description: The OAuth access token is inserted directly into the query string of a GET request to Google's user-info endpoint. Query-string tokens can be exposed through browser history, intermediary access logs, monitoring, and referrer handling. Anyone obtaining the token may be able to call the OAuth provider or access resources granted by its scopes. The test's exact URL expectation demonstrates that the service uses this token transport.

title: Unbounded verdict request payload permits resource exhaustion
description: The exported `check` method accepts an arbitrary `key` string and `selectedLines` array from a caller outside this file and forwards them without any length, count, or serialized-body limit. title: Identity mock disables HTML sanitization in security tests
description: The test replaces Angular's DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustHtml with an identity function, returning arbitrary HTML unchanged. Feedback comments supplied to populateSlideshowFromFeedbacks are therefore treated as already trusted in this test environment, so tests can pass even when attacker-controlled feedback would reach an HTML-rendering path without effective sanitization. title: Client-controlled review author enables identity spoofing

title: Unrestricted custom-file URL fetch enables SSRF and resource exhaustion
description: Startup customization accepts a configured URL and passes it directly to the file-download helper without restricting the destination to trusted origins, schemes, or non-private addresses. If an attacker can influence application customization configuration, they can cause the server to request internal services such as cloud metadata endpoints or administrative APIs. The same fetch has no visible response-size, timeout, or download-count limit, allowing a configured remote resource to consume excessive bandwidth, disk, or startup time.

retrieveCustomFile reads the configured property and treats any value recognized as a URL as a remote file source. No trusted-origin allow-list or private-network validation is present.

The configured URL is passed to utils.downloadToFile, causing the server to make an outbound request and write the response without any visible destination restriction, response-size limit, or timeout control.

title: Unescaped application name causes stored HTML/script injection
description: The configured application name is interpolated directly into an HTML title element and written into the deployed index.html. An attacker who can influence the customization configuration can inject markup or script into the generated page, resulting in stored XSS for users loading the application. No HTML-context escaping or safe text replacement is applied.

title: Unescaped cookie-consent configuration enables frontend injection
description: Cookie-consent configuration values, including message text and link URL, are concatenated into an HTML/JavaScript configuration fragment and written to index.html without context-appropriate escaping or URL-scheme validation. A malicious value containing quotes or markup can break the generated structure and inject script, while a javascript: link URL can execute when users activate the banner. The render/execution occurs when the generated frontend is loaded, outside this file.

title: Special memories can bypass required user association
description: The validator intends to ensure that mandatory special memories belong to their designated users (`john` or `emma`), but its predicate only flags a memory when `memory.user` is truthy and different from the expected user. A special memory with both required security-question fields set and no `user` value bypasses this check, despite the error message stating that it must belong to the designated user. If an attacker or untrusted configuration source can supply the memory configuration, this permits a challenge memory to be detached from the required account and can subvert the intended stalking/challenge workflow.

trace.description: The exported validator receives `memories` from a caller outside this file, or falls back to the configured `memories` collection; these values determine which records are treated as mandatory special memories.

The validator identifies a special memory only when both special fields are truthy, so a caller-controlled/configured memory with the required fields can enter this validation path even if its `user` field is absent.

The check requires `memory.user` to be truthy before comparing it with the expected user. Therefore `user: undefined` or an omitted user is not added to `matchingMemories`, and validation succeeds instead of enforcing the stated `john`/`emma` association.

title: Unvalidated server-side fetch enables SSRF
description: The exported `checkIfDomainReachable` function accepts an arbitrary URL from callers outside this file and passes it directly to Node's server-side `fetch` without parsing, scheme restrictions, hostname allow-listing, or private-network/IP validation. A caller able to influence `domain` can make the server issue requests to loopback services, cloud metadata endpoints, internal admin APIs, or other network resources reachable from the server. The five-second timeout limits individual request duration but does not prevent SSRF or sufficiently repeated requests.

title: Unvalidated webhook URL enables server-side request forgery

title: XML external entity resolution enables arbitrary local file disclosure
description: The exported parser accepts caller-controlled XML and deliberately enables DTD loading and entity substitution. It also registers libxml2 filesystem input providers, allowing external entities such as file:///etc/passwd to be resolved. An attacker who supplies XML containing an external entity can therefore cause local file contents to be read and returned in the serialized XML, without any allow-list or external-entity restriction. The VM timeout limits entity-expansion hangs but does not prevent file disclosure or other XXE effects.

title: BasketItem CRUD exposes caller-controlled basket ownership and sensitive fields
description: The BasketItem model exposes all declared attributes to the generated CRUD surface without an explicit request-field allow-list or model-level authorization constraint. Because BasketId is caller-controlled and the model contains no ownership relation or per-basket restriction, an authenticated or otherwise reachable caller may create or modify an item belonging to another user's basket, and can alter quantity or product association. The CRUD caller and authorization logic are outside this file, so endpoint-level controls cannot be confirmed here.

title: User-controlled UserId enables unauthorized memory data export
description: The data-export handler authenticates the caller but does not bind the memory lookup to the authenticated user's ID. Instead, it trusts the caller-controlled `req.body.UserId`. User A can submit User B's ID and receive User B's memory records, including image URLs and captions, in the export response. This is a broken object-level authorization issue and also reflects a server-side trust violation: the resource owner is taken from the request rather than derived from the authenticated identity.

trace.description: POST /rest/user/data-export invokes the exported handler; the route has authentication middleware, but the caller and any body field validation are outside this file.
The handler confirms that some bearer token maps to a logged-in user, but it does not compare the authenticated user's ID with the request's `UserId` value.

The memory query uses `req.body.UserId` directly as the owner filter. An authenticated attacker can substitute another user's ID; there is no per-resource ownership check between the lookup and response construction.
The resulting memory records are copied into the exported response, exposing the selected user's image URLs and captions to the caller.

title: Unbounded data export permits excessive resource consumption
description: The authenticated data-export endpoint performs multiple potentially large database reads without pagination, result limits, or an application-level rate limit visible in this handler. `findAll` can load all memories for the supplied user, while the orders and reviews queries can return unbounded collections; the records are then mapped and serialized into one response. Repeated requests or a user with a large dataset can consume substantial database, CPU, memory, and response bandwidth resources.

trace.description: POST /rest/user/data-export enters this handler; the caller and any infrastructure-level throttling are outside this file.
The handler issues a collection-wide memory query with no limit, offset, or pagination control.
It also queries orders and reviews without visible limits or pagination, allowing entire collections for the account to be loaded.

All returned records are mapped into `userData` and serialized with `JSON.stringify` into a single response, multiplying memory and CPU use for large datasets and allowing repeated requests to pressure the service.

title: Security-question verification bypass on data erasure
description: The data-erasure form declares a security answer input, and the GET handler retrieves the authenticated user's security question, but the POST handler never verifies `req.body.securityAnswer` (or the submitted email). Any authenticated user can submit an arbitrary or empty answer and immediately create a deletion request for their account. This bypasses the apparent security-question step protecting an irreversible, sensitive operation.

trace.description: POST `/` receives the data-erasure form fields from an external caller; the caller and route mounting are outside this file.
The request type includes `email` and `securityAnswer`, but the handler only checks whether a session token maps to an authenticated user. It does not validate either submitted field.
The handler creates a privacy/deletion request solely from `loggedInUser.data.id`, without checking the security answer or requiring any additional verification.

title: Unbounded creation of privacy-request records
description: Every authenticated request to the data-erasure POST endpoint inserts a new `PrivacyRequestModel` row. There is no visible rate limit, idempotency check, duplicate suppression, or other quota on this write operation. An attacker with a valid account can automate requests and create an unbounded number of deletion-request records, consuming database storage and processing capacity. Deployment-level throttling may mitigate this, but no control is present in this file.

trace.description: POST `/` receives externally supplied data and can be invoked repeatedly; the route's mounting and any infrastructure controls are outside this file.
The handler authenticates the caller but performs no rate-limit, replay, duplicate, or per-user quota check before processing the request.
Each request unconditionally persists another deletion request, allowing repeated authenticated calls to grow the `PrivacyRequestModel` table without bound.

title: No visible audit logging for data-erasure requests
description: The handler performs a security-relevant account/data-erasure action but contains no audit logging for the request, the authenticated user, or the resulting deletion-request creation. If this route is the only execution path for the operation, investigators cannot reliably reconstruct who requested erasure or detect automated abuse. Logging could exist in middleware or the model layer outside this file, so confidence is moderate.

trace.description: The POST data-erasure route receives an externally initiated request; route registration and surrounding middleware are outside this file.
After authentication, the handler proceeds directly to persistence and cookie removal without emitting an audit event or security log.
The privacy request is created with no accompanying log of the user, request, or operation result.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of asset from private directory
description: The easter-egg handler is reachable through an unauthenticated GET route and unconditionally serves a file located under a directory explicitly named `private`. No authentication or authorization check is performed before the file is returned. An anonymous caller can request the route and obtain the private Three.js demo asset, potentially disclosing internal frontend functionality or challenge material.

trace.description: The caller reaches the exported `serveEasterEgg` handler through `GET /the/devs/are/so/funny/they/hid/an/easter/egg/within/the/easter/egg`; the route is registered without authentication or authorization middleware. The route registration is outside this file.
The handler accepts the incoming request and proceeds directly to the response operation without checking authentication, authorization, role, or any other access condition.
`res.sendFile` unconditionally serves `frontend/dist/frontend/assets/private/threejs-demo.html`, exposing the private-directory asset to any unauthenticated requester.

title: Public exposure of KeePass credential database
description: The public file-serving middleware explicitly permits downloading `incident-support.kdbx`, a KeePass database, without any authentication or authorization check in this code path. A caller reaching the middleware can request `/.../incident-support.kdbx`, pass the allow check, and receive the file through `res.sendFile`. Disclosure of the database can expose stored credentials and enable account compromise if the database is accessible or crackable.

trace.description: The exported middleware receives the attacker-controlled request and route parameters; the route registration/caller is outside this file.
The requested filename is taken directly from `params.file` and only checked for a forward slash. No authentication, authorization, or sensitivity check is performed before the filename is validated.
The condition explicitly allowlists `incident-support.kdbx` in addition to ordinary document extensions, allowing a request for that database to proceed.
The permitted filename is sent from the server's `ftp/` directory to the requester. This is the disclosure sink for the sensitive KeePass database.

title: Platform-dependent path traversal in public file server
description: Path traversal protection rejects only `/`, while the filesystem path is constructed with `path.resolve`, which uses the host platform's path separator. On Windows, a filename such as `..\\..\\secret.pdf` contains no forward slash, passes the separator check and `.pdf` suffix check, and can resolve outside the `ftp/` directory. The attacker can therefore retrieve files outside the intended public directory when the application runs on Windows, subject only to the required filename suffix.

trace.description: The exported middleware receives `params.file` from an external request; the route handler invoking this middleware is outside this file.
The attacker-controlled filename is rejected only when it contains a forward slash. Backslash separators are not rejected, so Windows traversal sequences such as `..\\..\\secret.pdf` remain possible.
The suffix check accepts attacker-selected names ending in `.md` or `.pdf`; it does not canonicalize the path or verify that the resolved path remains under `ftp/`.
`path.resolve('ftp/', file)` canonicalizes the attacker-controlled path and may resolve it outside `ftp/` on Windows, after which `sendFile` returns the resulting file.

title: Deluxe membership payment can be bypassed with an unsupported payment mode
description: An authenticated customer can obtain deluxe membership without supplying either a valid wallet payment or a valid card payment. The handler only performs payment checks when `paymentMode` is exactly `wallet` or `card`; any other value, including an omitted value, reaches the role update. The attacker can then receive a deluxe authorization token and premium privileges without paying.

trace.description: The exported upgrade handler receives the attacker-controlled request; the route caller and authentication middleware are outside this file.
The handler accepts `req.body.paymentMode` and branches into payment validation only for the literal values `wallet` and `card`. There is no rejection path for any other value.
The card-specific validation is likewise conditional and is skipped when the caller submits another payment mode or omits the field.
After the conditional payment logic completes, the handler unconditionally changes the selected customer to the deluxe role and issues a new authorization token.

title: Missing wallet record is treated as a successful payment
description: The wallet payment path allows a customer with no wallet record to become deluxe for free. When `WalletModel.findOne` returns null, the condition at line 26 is false and execution enters the `else` branch; the decrement affects no wallet rows but the handler still proceeds to grant the deluxe role and token.

For `paymentMode === 'wallet'`, the handler looks up a wallet using the request's user identifier.
A missing wallet is not rejected: the insufficient-funds check only rejects when `wallet != null` and the balance is below 49.
The `else` branch decrements the balance for the user, but when no wallet exists this updates zero rows and does not establish that payment occurred.
The handler nevertheless updates the user to the deluxe role and returns a newly authorized token.

title: Card payment is validated but never charged
description: The card payment path verifies only that the submitted card belongs to the selected customer and is not expired. It never charges, debits, or otherwise records a card payment before granting deluxe membership. Any customer with an unexpired stored card can repeatedly activate the premium role without a corresponding payment transaction.

trace.description: The exported upgrade handler receives the external request; the route caller is outside this file.
The card branch looks up a card by the caller-supplied payment identifier and the selected user's identifier.
The only card controls are existence, ownership through `UserId`, and expiration checks; there is no payment-provider charge, balance deduction, or payment confirmation.
After the card checks pass, the code directly changes the user's role to deluxe and creates a new authorization token.

title: CAPTCHA answer disclosed in API response
description: The CAPTCHA endpoint returns the server-generated CAPTCHA answer in the JSON response alongside the image. An authenticated attacker can request a CAPTCHA, read `answer` directly from the response, and submit that value to any flow protected by `verifyImageCaptcha`, defeating the CAPTCHA challenge entirely. This is a broken authentication-control design because the challenge secret is disclosed to the client.

trace.description: The caller outside this file invokes the exported `imageCaptchas()` handler for `GET /rest/image-captcha`; the route itself has no framework authentication middleware, although the handler performs an authentication check.
The handler generates a CAPTCHA and stores both its image and answer in the server-side record associated with the authenticated user.
The response serializes the complete `imageCaptcha` object, including the secret `answer` field, to the requester.

title: Missing CAPTCHA is treated as successful verification
description: `verifyImageCaptcha` allows the protected request to continue when no recent CAPTCHA exists because the condition is `!captchas[0] || ...`. Therefore, a caller can omit the CAPTCHA-generation step, allow the record to expire or be absent, and still reach `next()` without proving any challenge. The route is used for `POST /rest/user/data-export`, so the CAPTCHA protection can be bypassed outright.

trace.description: The caller outside this file invokes the exported `verifyImageCaptcha` middleware for `POST /rest/user/data-export`; this file receives the request and its body through the exported middleware parameters.
The middleware derives the user identity and queries for the most recent CAPTCHA belonging to that user within the previous five minutes.
The verification condition treats an absent CAPTCHA record as success: when `captchas[0]` is missing, the left side of the OR expression is true regardless of the submitted answer.
The middleware calls `next()`, allowing the protected operation to proceed without any CAPTCHA proof.

title: Unrestricted CAPTCHA generation and persistence
description: The authenticated CAPTCHA-generation endpoint performs CPU work to generate an image and persists a new database row for every request, but this file shows no per-user, per-IP, or per-endpoint rate limit and no quota. An authenticated attacker can repeatedly call `GET /rest/image-captcha` to consume image-generation CPU and grow the `ImageCaptchaModel` table, potentially degrading service. Reverse-proxy controls may mitigate this, but no application-level protection is visible here.

trace.description: The caller outside this file exposes `imageCaptchas()` as `GET /rest/image-captcha`; no rate-limiting middleware is declared for the route.
Each request dynamically loads the CAPTCHA library and generates a five-character noisy color CAPTCHA, consuming CPU and memory.
The generated image and answer are built into a new model instance for every request.
Every generated CAPTCHA is saved as a new database record, with no visible quota, cleanup, or request-frequency control.

title: Windows path traversal allows arbitrary file disclosure
description: The file-serving handler accepts an attacker-controlled path parameter and only rejects forward slashes before passing it to `path.resolve()` and `res.sendFile()`. On Windows, backslashes are path separators, so a value such as `..\..\config\秘密` (with an appropriate route encoding) can escape the `encryptionkeys/` directory and cause arbitrary readable files to be returned. The check does not verify that the resolved path remains beneath the intended directory or use an explicit filename allow-list.

trace.description: The exported `serveKeyFiles` function receives the Express request from a caller/route outside this file and returns the request handler; the attacker-controlled route parameter is therefore introduced through `Request.params` here.
The handler copies the attacker-controlled `params.file` value without canonicalization or an allow-list.
The only validation rejects `/`. It does not reject Windows backslash separators, dot segments, absolute paths, or verify the canonical result remains inside `encryptionkeys/`.

The unchecked value is joined with the key directory using platform-sensitive `path.resolve()` and passed to `res.sendFile()`. On Windows, a backslash traversal such as `..\\..\\config\\secret` can resolve outside `encryptionkeys/`, exposing arbitrary readable files.

title: ZIP extraction allows path traversal outside the complaints directory
description: The unauthenticated POST /file-upload route accepts attacker-controlled ZIP archives and extracts each entry to disk. The containment check is incorrect: it tests whether the resolved path merely contains the current working directory, rather than verifying that it is within the intended uploads/complaints directory. A path such as ../outside.txt or ../../app-file can resolve inside the application working directory while escaping uploads/complaints, and is then written using the traversal-containing path. This permits unauthorized file creation or overwriting wherever the process has write access.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: the exported handler receives the unauthenticated POST /file-upload upload request through Express and reads the uploaded file from Request.file.
For files whose attacker-controlled originalname ends in .zip, the handler passes the complete attacker-controlled upload buffer to extractZipBuffer.

The ZIP entry path is attacker-controlled and is concatenated into a filesystem path. The check only requires the resolved path to contain the process current directory, which does not establish containment within uploads/complaints; traversal to sibling paths inside the working directory passes.
The archive entry is written to the traversal-containing relative path without canonical-path containment enforcement, allowing files outside uploads/complaints to be created or overwritten.

title: Unauthenticated file upload lacks size and archive-expansion limits
description: The file-upload processing path has no effective upload-size control. checkUploadSize is registered in the /file-upload middleware chain but its implementation is empty and always calls next(). ZIP processing then loads the complete upload into memory, enumerates every archive entry, and streams decompressed content to disk without limits on input size, entry count, expanded size, or total disk usage. An unauthenticated attacker can repeatedly submit very large files or highly expanding archives to consume memory, CPU, and disk space.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file: unauthenticated POST /file-upload requests reach the file middleware chain and provide attacker-controlled file content.
The nominal upload-size middleware performs no validation or limiting and unconditionally continues processing.
ZIP processing receives the complete attacker-controlled Buffer and opens it in memory, with no visible maximum upload, archive, entry-count, or decompressed-size limit.
Every archive entry is streamed and written to disk without aggregate size or count limits, enabling decompression bombs and disk exhaustion.

title: Unauthenticated language endpoint performs unbounded concurrent file processing
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/languages endpoint performs an unbounded directory enumeration and launches a concurrent read and JSON.parse operation for every file found. There is no pagination, result cap, caching, timeout, or route-level rate limiting visible in this handler. An attacker can repeatedly request the endpoint, causing disk I/O, concurrent promise/memory growth, and CPU consumption proportional to the number and size of translation files. The route registration and any infrastructure-level throttling are outside this file, so those controls cannot be confirmed here.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller/router outside this file invokes the exported getLanguageList handler for GET /rest/languages; the route is unauthenticated.
The handler enumerates every file in the translations directory without imposing a count limit or selecting a bounded subset.

For each enumerated filename, the handler concurrently reads the file and parses its complete contents as JSON. Promise.all later waits for all these operations, allowing per-request resource use to grow with the directory contents and file sizes.
All language-processing promises are materialized and awaited at once, with no rate limit, pagination, concurrency bound, or response-size limit in this code path.

title: Log-file serving handler lacks visible authorization control
description: The exported handler accepts the attacker-controlled `params.file` value and serves a file from the server's `logs/` directory without performing any authentication, role, or authorization check in this function. If this helper is mounted on a publicly reachable route without external middleware, an attacker can read application log files, which may contain internal diagnostics, PII, tokens, or other sensitive operational data. The caller and any upstream middleware are outside this file, so reachability and compensating authorization cannot be confirmed here.

title: Windows path traversal bypasses forward-slash filename check
description: The validation rejects only the forward-slash character, but the value is then interpreted by `path.resolve` using the host operating system's path rules. On Windows, an attacker can submit a value such as `..\\.env` or `C:\\Windows\\win.ini`; it contains no forward slash, passes the check, and causes `sendFile` to read outside the intended `logs/` directory. This enables arbitrary local file disclosure, subject to the process account's read permissions.

`path.resolve` and `sendFile` interpret the attacker-controlled value with platform path semantics, allowing a Windows traversal or absolute-path filename to escape `logs/`.

title: Race condition bypasses one-like-per-user rule and corrupts review like state
description: The handler enforces the one-like-per-user rule with a non-atomic check-then-update sequence. Two concurrent requests for the same review and authenticated user can both observe that the user's email is absent at line 31, both increment likesCount, and then independently read, append, and write likedBy after the artificial delay. Depending on interleaving, this can create duplicate likes, make likesCount disagree with likedBy, or cause one user's concurrently added like to be overwritten. An attacker can issue concurrent POST requests with the same review id to subvert the intended business rule and corrupt review-like state.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the attacker-controlled request from the POST /rest/products/reviews route; the route caller and any outer middleware are outside this file.
The target review identifier is taken from req.body.id, and the authenticated user's email is obtained from the request.
The handler looks up the review by the caller-supplied id, without an atomic condition tying the subsequent mutation to the user's absence from likedBy.
The handler checks likedBy.includes(user.data.email) and rejects only if a prior request has already recorded the email. Concurrent requests can pass this check before either records the like.
The likesCount increment is performed separately from the duplicate-prevention check and likedBy update, so concurrent requests can independently increment the count.

After a fixed delay, the handler reads the review again and appends the user's email to the in-memory likedBy array. The delay widens the race window, and this read/append is not protected by an atomic conditional update.
The modified array is written back with an unconditional $set. Concurrent requests can write duplicate emails or overwrite each other's changes, producing inconsistent persisted like state.

title: Unthrottled authenticated like endpoint performs forced delay and multiple database operations
description: Each authenticated request deliberately sleeps for 150 ms and performs multiple database operations, while this handler contains no per-user, per-IP, or per-endpoint rate limit or concurrency control. An attacker with a valid account can generate many concurrent requests to occupy application resources and database connections/operations. External infrastructure may mitigate this, but no such control is visible in this file.

The handler only verifies that a user is authenticated before continuing; no rate-limit or concurrency-limit check is present in the visible code.
A request performs a review lookup followed by multiple database updates/lookups, increasing the cost of each accepted request.
Every accepted request unconditionally waits 150 ms, allowing many concurrent authenticated requests to consume request-handling and timer resources while also retaining the in-flight operation.

title: Unauthenticated access to all memories and associated users
description: The unauthenticated GET endpoint retrieves every memory and eagerly includes the associated UserModel, then returns the complete result set to any caller. If memories or associated user records are intended to be user-scoped, an unauthenticated attacker can enumerate other users' records and any non-excluded UserModel attributes. No authentication, authorization, or filtering is present in this file.

The unrestricted memory collection and included user records are serialized directly into the HTTP response for the unauthenticated caller.

title: Caller-controlled UserId is persisted on new memories
description: addMemory constructs a persistence record using req.body.UserId, a caller-controlled property, and passes it to MemoryModel.create. UserId is an ownership-sensitive field: if the appendUserId middleware does not overwrite or strictly validate it, an authenticated user can submit another user's identifier and create a memory attributed to that user, violating object ownership and potentially causing unauthorized content to appear in another user's collection. The middleware implementation is outside this file, so exploitability depends on its behavior.

The handler copies req.body.UserId directly into the new record rather than deriving the ownership field from a trusted authenticated identity. The appendUserId middleware is outside this file and its overwrite behavior cannot be confirmed here.
The record, including the caller-supplied UserId, is persisted by MemoryModel.create without an explicit ownership or field-authorization check in this handler.

title: Unbounded unauthenticated memory listing
description: The unauthenticated memories listing has no pagination, limit, or other result-size bound. A caller can repeatedly request GET /rest/memories and force the application to load every memory and associated user into memory and serialize the entire collection, causing excessive database, memory, and response bandwidth consumption as the dataset grows.

The complete result set is materialized and returned in one JSON response, allowing repeated requests to consume database, application memory, CPU, and network resources.

title: Unauthenticated exposure of sensitive application metrics
description: The unauthenticated GET /metrics route exposes the Prometheus registry directly. The registry includes sensitive internal and business metrics such as total digital wallet balance, registered-user counts, order and review counts, complaints, feedback, and cheat-score information. Any unauthenticated remote caller can scrape these values, enabling business intelligence disclosure and reconnaissance of application state. No authentication or authorization check is performed before the registry is returned.

The handler sets the Prometheus content type and invokes the global registry serializer, with no access-control check or restriction to an internal monitoring network.

The serialized registry is written directly to the HTTP response. The registry contains metrics populated elsewhere in this file, including wallet balance at line 148, user totals at lines 136-145, and order, review, feedback, complaint, and cheat-score metrics at lines 120-155 and 206-213.

title: SQL injection in login credential query
description: The unauthenticated POST /rest/user/login handler receives the caller-controlled email from req.body and interpolates it directly into a raw SQL query. An attacker can submit an email such as `' OR 1=1 --` to alter the WHERE clause, potentially causing authentication as an arbitrary first matching user and bypassing password verification. No parameterization or allow-listing is present.

title: No visible rate limiting on password authentication
description: The public login endpoint performs password hashing and a database query for every request, but this file applies no per-IP, per-account, or per-endpoint throttling, lockout, or other abuse control. An attacker can send unlimited login attempts, consuming CPU in security.hash and database capacity while also enabling credential-stuffing or brute-force attacks. Controls outside this file may partially mitigate the issue, but none are visible in this route.

Each request invokes security.hash on the supplied password and constructs an authentication database lookup, regardless of whether previous attempts from the same source or account have failed.
The raw database query is executed for every login attempt, with no rate-limit, lockout, attempt counter, or other local throttling control before the expensive authentication work.

title: Login successes and failures are not logged in the handler

The failure branch returns a 401 response and the success branch issues a token, but neither path records the event or an account/source identifier for detection and investigation. A centralized logger elsewhere could mitigate this gap, so the finding is limited to the control absent from this file.

The handler performs credential verification and branches on whether a matching user was found.
A valid user proceeds directly to token creation and response without a security-event log entry.
Invalid credentials produce a 401 response directly, with no failed-login event recorded for monitoring or alerting.

title: NFT verification trusts caller-supplied wallet address without proof of ownership
description: The NFT verification endpoint authenticates neither the caller nor control of the wallet. It accepts an arbitrary walletAddress from the request body and treats membership in a process-global set as proof that the current caller owns that wallet. Because NFT mint events and wallet addresses are observable on-chain, an attacker can submit another user's recently minted address and receive a successful challenge result; the endpoint then deletes the address from the shared set. No wallet signature, nonce, session binding, or other proof of key possession is required.

The handler receives the caller-controlled request body and copies req.body.walletAddress into metamaskAddress without validating its format, binding it to a session, or requiring a cryptographic signature.

The handler uses the supplied address as the sole authentication/authorization condition. Any address present in the global addressesMinted set is accepted, and the success response grants the challenge status while removing that address from the set. There is no proof that the requester controls the corresponding private key.

title: Unbounded payment-card listing can consume excessive resources
description: The authenticated GET /api/Cards handler retrieves every payment card for the current user with an unbounded CardModel.findAll call and returns the complete result set in one response. There is no pagination, maximum result count, or other application-level bound in this file. If an account accumulates a large number of cards, a single request can force the application to load and serialize all of them, consuming database, memory, CPU, and response bandwidth. title: Unauthenticated access to premium content bypasses paywall
description: The premium-content handler is reachable through GET /this/page/is/hidden/behind/an/incredibly/high/paywall/that/could/only/be/unlocked/by/sending/1btc/to/us without authentication or authorization middleware. The handler unconditionally sends the private Juice Shop wallpaper from the filesystem, allowing any caller to download the premium content.

An authorized accounting account, or an attacker who compromises such an account, can repeatedly invoke the endpoint to force the database to return all orders and the application to allocate and process the full result set, causing excessive memory, CPU, database, and response bandwidth consumption as order volume grows.
