title: Unauthenticated exposure of asset from private directory
description: The unauthenticated GET route exposes a file located under the application's `frontend/dist/frontend/assets/private/` directory. The handler performs no authentication or authorization check and always sends the file, so any remote caller who knows or discovers the route can retrieve an asset designated as private. This is an access-control failure and an exposed-internal-resource security misconfiguration; the impact depends on the contents of `thank-you.jpg`, but the route provides no protection for a resource stored in a private path.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller outside this file registers `servePrivacyPolicyProof()` for `GET /we/may/also/instruct/you/to/refuse/all/reasonably/necessary/responsibility` with no authentication middleware.
The exported handler accepts the Express request and response but does not inspect authentication state, user identity, or permissions before serving the resource.
The handler sends the fixed file from a directory explicitly named `private` to the unauthenticated caller via `res.sendFile()`.

title: Unauthenticated checkout of arbitrary baskets
description: The checkout route is registered without authentication, accepts an arbitrary basket identifier, and loads that basket without checking ownership or associating it with the authenticated customer. The handler then destroys all basket items and creates an order for the selected basket. An attacker can submit another user's basket ID to check out and consume their basket. Additionally, the wallet/payment block is optional, so a request can create an order with a null payment ID without demonstrating payment.

trace.description: POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout enters the exported handler; the caller and route registration are outside this file, and the route is declared with no authentication middleware.
The basket target is taken directly from the attacker-controlled path parameter.
The handler retrieves the basket solely by the supplied ID and includes its products; there is no owner, user, or session constraint.
The authenticated customer, when present, is used only to derive an email/order identifier; no authorization check compares that customer to the basket owner.
After processing, the handler destroys every item in the selected basket and inserts the resulting order, while payment handling is conditional on an optional request-body UserId/payment combination.
The order is persisted even when paymentId is absent or null, allowing the unauthenticated caller to complete an order without a verified payment.

title: Caller-controlled UserId targets wallet mutations
description: The request body controls UserId, which is used as the target of wallet debit and credit operations. No server-derived identity is used and there is no authorization check binding UserId to the authenticated caller. An attacker can select another user's ID and request wallet payment to debit that user's wallet, or select an account to receive the order's bonus points. This is caller control over a sensitive authorization/property field rather than a trusted identity.

trace.description: The exported checkout handler receives request data from the unauthenticated route; the external caller is outside this file.
The handler branches on and trusts the request-body UserId as the identity for financial wallet operations, rather than deriving it from the authenticated session.
For wallet payment, the supplied UserId selects the wallet record and the supplied paymentId selects the wallet-payment path, with no ownership or authorization check.
The selected user's wallet is debited using a WHERE clause containing only the attacker-controlled UserId.
The same attacker-selected UserId is used to credit bonus points, allowing bonus attribution and financial effects to be redirected to an arbitrary account.

title: Replayable and forgeable campaign coupon discounts
description: The coupon fallback accepts a base64-encoded coupon code and date from the request. It checks only whether the supplied date equals the campaign's fixed validOn timestamp; it does not check that the campaign is currently active, that the coupon is signed, or that it has not already been redeemed. Because the campaign records contain historical dates, an attacker can construct a payload such as a known campaign code plus its published timestamp and repeatedly obtain the associated discount, including the 75% campaign.

trace.description: The checkout handler receives externally supplied request data; the route caller is outside this file.
Discount calculation is invoked during checkout and can use coupon data from the request when the basket has no accepted coupon.
The handler reads attacker-controlled couponData from the request body and base64-decodes it without any authenticity or redemption-state check.
The decoded fields are treated as a coupon code and numeric date, and the code selects a campaign entry.
A discount is granted when the supplied date merely equals the campaign's historical validOn value; there is no current-date, signature, or one-time-use validation.

title: Unauthenticated checkout enables repeated PDF and database resource consumption
description: This unauthenticated endpoint performs expensive work for every request: dynamically loading PDFKit, creating a PDF and filesystem write, and executing per-product inventory queries and updates in a loop. No rate limit, request quota, basket-size cap, or idempotency control is present in this handler. Repeated requests, especially against a basket containing many products, can consume CPU, filesystem I/O, database connections, and concurrent processing capacity.

trace.description: POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout reaches the exported handler without authentication; route registration is outside this file.
Each request performs a basket lookup and processes the selected basket regardless of caller identity, with no visible throttling or request-level quota.
The handler dynamically loads PDFKit and creates a filesystem-backed PDF output for each checkout request.
The PDF is written to disk, while the preceding product loop performs database quantity lookups and updates for each basket item; no size or count limit is enforced.

title: Unauthenticated memory-backed upload permits resource exhaustion
description: The upload route performs memory-backed file handling before authenticating the caller. The external route middleware `uploadToMemory.single('file')` supplies `req.file`, and this handler immediately retains the complete uploaded buffer and passes it to `fileType.fromBuffer` without any size or rate-limit control visible in this file. Authentication is checked only afterward. An unauthenticated attacker can repeatedly submit large multipart files, causing memory consumption in the upload middleware and additional CPU/memory use during type detection, potentially degrading or exhausting the service. Any infrastructure or middleware limit would reduce the impact, but no such control is shown here.

trace.description: POST /profile/image/file reaches the exported handler through an external caller and the `uploadToMemory.single('file')` middleware; the request is not protected by route-level authentication.
The handler accepts the middleware-provided file and obtains its entire in-memory buffer before checking whether the caller is authenticated.
The complete attacker-supplied buffer is processed by file-type detection, adding CPU and memory work for every unauthenticated upload attempt.

The uploaded buffer is written to disk; repeated large uploads can also consume filesystem capacity if authentication is bypassed or a valid session is used, and no per-request size, count, or rate limit is enforced in this handler.

title: Authenticated SSRF through profile image URL fetch
description: The handler accepts `req.body.imageUrl` and passes it directly to `fetch` without validating its scheme, hostname, port, resolved IP, or destination origin. An authenticated attacker can submit URLs targeting loopback services, cloud metadata endpoints, internal administrative APIs, or other network resources reachable from the server. The response is then consumed by the application, confirming a server-side request primitive.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the attacker-controlled request object from the caller and reads the externally supplied `imageUrl` body field; the route is registered outside this file.
The request body value is assigned to `url` and only checked for a challenge-marker substring. This check does not restrict the destination or validate the URL.
The handler only checks whether the supplied token maps to a logged-in user. It performs no authorization of the destination represented by `url`.
The user-controlled URL is used as the target of a server-side `fetch` call without an allow-list or internal-network protection. An attacker can cause the server to request internal HTTP resources.

title: Unbounded remote response download enables resource exhaustion
description: The endpoint performs an outbound fetch and streams the entire response into a server-side file, but this file contains no response-size limit, timeout, rate limiting, or content-length enforcement. An authenticated attacker can repeatedly submit URLs serving very large or never-ending responses, causing sustained network, memory/stream, disk, and file-descriptor consumption. The redirect behavior of `fetch` can also make the final destination attacker-controlled unless constrained elsewhere.

trace.description: The exported handler receives attacker-controlled request data from the caller outside this file and exposes the profile-image URL operation.
The attacker-controlled `imageUrl` is copied into `url` without a size, scheme, host, or response-policy restriction.
The server initiates a remote request using the supplied URL, with no visible timeout, maximum response size, or request throttling.
The complete response body is converted to a stream and written to a file. A large or unbounded response can consume server network bandwidth, disk space, stream resources, and processing capacity.

title: Unvalidated remote content stored as a publicly served profile image
description: The fetched remote response is persisted under a publicly served uploads directory based only on the URL's final extension. The response's actual content type and content are not validated, and SVG is explicitly permitted. A malicious server can return attacker-controlled SVG or other active content while using an allowed extension, causing untrusted content to be stored as a public profile asset and potentially rendered by browsers in a security-sensitive origin. This is an unsafe remote file-handling and content-integrity boundary; the eventual browser rendering occurs outside this file.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the caller-controlled profile image URL through the request object; route registration and any browser rendering are outside this file.
The handler derives the stored file extension from the untrusted URL string and allows `svg` alongside raster image extensions, without inspecting the response content or Content-Type.
The arbitrary remote response body is written directly to the application's public uploads directory under a predictable user-specific filename.

The stored path is persisted as the user's profile image URL. A later renderer outside this file may serve or embed the attacker-controlled content, including malicious SVG markup, from the application's asset origin.

title: Windows path traversal allows unauthorized local file reads
description: The handler attempts to restrict callers to a single quarantine-file component by rejecting only forward slashes. On Windows, backslashes are path separators, so a value such as `..\\..\\.env` or an absolute drive path can pass the check and be resolved outside `ftp/quarantine/`. `res.sendFile` then reads and returns the attacker-selected file, enabling unauthorized local file disclosure. The issue is platform-dependent: on POSIX systems backslashes are ordinary filename characters, but this code is unsafe when deployed on Windows.

trace.description: The exported middleware receives the Express request from a caller outside this file; the attacker-controlled route parameter is available as `params.file`.
The requested file name is copied directly from `params.file` without canonicalization or an allow-list.
The only validation rejects the `/` character. It does not reject Windows backslash separators, `..` path components, or Windows absolute paths.

The unchecked value is passed to `path.resolve` and then to `res.sendFile`. On Windows, traversal input such as `..\\..\\secret.txt` can resolve outside the quarantine directory and the resulting file is returned to the caller.

title: Unauthenticated access to arbitrary recycle items
description: The recycle-item endpoint is reachable without authentication and retrieves a record solely from the caller-controlled path parameter. There is no per-user ownership or authorization check before returning the matching record. An unauthenticated attacker can request `/api/Recycles/<victim-recycle-id>` and receive another user's recycle item data, constituting broken object-level access control and unauthorized resource disclosure.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the HTTP request from its caller outside this file; the architecture registers it as unauthenticated `GET /api/Recycles/:id`.
The handler reads the attacker-controlled `req.params.id` path parameter and converts it to a lookup value without deriving or checking an authenticated user identity or ownership relationship.

`RecycleModel.findAll` queries by the supplied ID and the resulting record is sent directly in the response. No authorization check occurs between lookup and response, allowing arbitrary resource-ID substitution.

title: Unauthenticated repetition of notifications for arbitrary solved challenges
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/repeat-notification endpoint accepts an arbitrary challenge name and triggers a notification for any solved challenge. The handler does not establish the caller's identity or verify that the caller is authorized to repeat that challenge's notification. An attacker can substitute another challenge's name and repeatedly invoke the notification side effect, potentially spamming clients or causing unauthorized notification activity.

trace.description: The exported handler receives an HTTP request from the caller outside this file. This function is registered as GET /rest/repeat-notification with no authentication middleware.
The caller-controlled query.challenge value is decoded and used as the target challenge name without any identity, ownership, or authorization data being checked.
The attacker-controlled challenge name is used to locate a challenge record. The lookup is not scoped to the current user and there is no authorization check after the lookup.

For any located challenge whose solved flag is true, the handler invokes sendNotification. Because the route is unauthenticated and accepts an arbitrary challenge name, an attacker can trigger this side effect for challenges they did not solve and repeat it at will.

title: Unauthenticated and forgeable challenge-progress restoration
description: All three restore-progress endpoints are reachable without authentication or authorization and trust a caller-supplied Hashids value to authorize challenge completion. The salts are hardcoded in source and Hashids provides obfuscation, not authenticity: an attacker who knows the salt and challenge IDs can generate valid continuation codes, or replay a code obtained elsewhere. The handler does not bind the code to a user, session, issuer, expiration, or signature. Submitting a forged code causes matching challenges to be marked solved through the global challenge state, allowing unauthenticated tampering with progress. The same defect is present in the FindIt and FixIt variants at lines 37-49 and 58-70.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller outside this file reaches the exported restoreProgress handler through PUT /rest/continue-code/apply/:continueCode with no authentication middleware; the attacker-controlled path parameter is received in the handler.
The handler constructs a Hashids decoder with a hardcoded salt and alphabet. This value is exposed in application source and is not a signature key or other authenticated-token mechanism.

The unauthenticated route takes continueCode directly from the request path and decodes it. The only validation is an alphanumeric regular expression, which does not establish authenticity, ownership, expiration, or intended recipient.
The supplied code is decoded into challenge IDs without any server-side verification that the code was issued to the current user or was cryptographically authenticated.
Decoded IDs are compared against the global challenge collection; there is no per-user ownership or authorization check between decoding and mutation.

Sink: every matching challenge is marked solved via challengeUtils.solve(challenge, true), mutating progress based solely on the unauthenticated, forgeable path value. The FindIt and FixIt handlers perform the equivalent mutation at lines 48 and 69.

title: SQL injection in product search query
description: The unauthenticated product-search handler copies the caller-controlled `q` query parameter into `criteria` and interpolates it directly into a raw SQL statement. The 200-character truncation limits length but does not provide SQL escaping or parameterization, so an attacker can terminate the string literal and inject SQL syntax, potentially altering the WHERE clause or causing database errors and data disclosure.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler receives an unauthenticated HTTP request for GET /rest/products/search.
The handler reads the attacker-controlled `q` query parameter and only truncates it to 200 characters. No SQL-specific validation or escaping is applied.
The untrusted value is embedded into a raw SQL template literal inside a LIKE expression and executed through `models.sequelize.query`; no bound parameter or allow-list intervenes.

title: Unbounded unauthenticated product search results
description: The public search endpoint performs a potentially expensive wildcard search with `LIKE '%...%'`, selects every column, and returns the entire matching result set without pagination, a result limit, or a visible rate limit. A request with an empty query (`q` omitted or equal to `undefined`) matches every non-deleted product, allowing repeated unauthenticated requests to consume database CPU, memory, and response bandwidth. Infrastructure-level throttling cannot be confirmed from this file.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; GET /rest/products/search is reachable without authentication according to the route registration, and this handler processes each request.
The query value defaults to an empty string when omitted, so the endpoint can be invoked without a restrictive search term.

The database query uses leading-wildcard LIKE predicates, selects all columns, and has no LIMIT or pagination clause. An empty criterion can match all non-deleted products, while no per-handler throttling is visible.

title: No rate limiting on unauthenticated password-reset attempts
description: The unauthenticated password-reset endpoint performs a database lookup, HMAC verification, and password update for every request, but no per-IP, per-account, or per-endpoint throttling is applied in this route. An attacker can repeatedly submit guesses for a user's security answer, causing repeated database/HMAC work and eventually resetting the password if a guess succeeds. The route is registered without authentication middleware, so application-level throttling is particularly important.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; this exported handler is registered as unauthenticated POST /rest/user/reset-password and receives attacker-controlled request data.
The handler accepts the target email, security-answer guess, and replacement password directly from the request body.

Each request queries for the account's security answer and compares the caller's answer using HMAC. There is no attempt counter, delay, lockout, or rate-limit check before this authentication decision.
After a successful answer guess, the handler changes the user's password. Repeated unauthenticated requests can therefore drive expensive authentication work and brute-force the reset factor.

title: Password reset relies solely on a reusable security answer
description: The password reset authorizes an irreversible credential change solely from an email address and a reusable security-question answer. The code does not issue or validate an expiring, one-time reset token, require a second recovery factor, or otherwise bind the reset to a fresh recovery transaction. If the answer is guessed, disclosed, or recovered from common personal information, an attacker can permanently take over the account; the absence of throttling makes guessing practical.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; the exported handler is reachable through unauthenticated POST /rest/user/reset-password.
The recovery identity and authentication factor are supplied directly by the caller as email and answer values.
The only visible authorization decision is whether HMAC(answer) equals the stored security-answer value; no expiring or one-time recovery credential is checked.
A matching reusable answer immediately authorizes replacement of the account password.

title: Password resets are not security-audited
description: The successful password-reset path changes a user's credential but contains no security audit log, event emission, or alerting. Because the endpoint is unauthenticated and can be brute-forced or abused after compromise of a security answer, the absence of a reset-success log prevents reliable detection and investigation of account-takeover attempts. No logging call is present between the reset request and password update in this file.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; this handler processes unauthenticated password-reset requests.
The handler receives the account email and recovery answer from the request body, establishing a security-relevant recovery attempt.
The answer is accepted and the target user is loaded for credential modification, but the path contains no audit-log or security-event call.
The password is updated without recording the successful reset or associated account and request context.

title: Untrusted client IP header stored without sanitization when XSS challenge is enabled
description: The GET /rest/saveLoginIp endpoint accepts the attacker-controlled `true-client-ip` request header. When `httpHeaderXssChallenge` is enabled, the code intentionally skips `security.sanitizeSecure`, then persists the header value as the authenticated user's `lastLoginIp`. An attacker can send a crafted value such as an HTML/script payload, which is stored in the user record and may execute as stored XSS when the login-IP field is later rendered by another component. The persistence point is present in this file; the eventual rendering sink is outside it.

trace.description: Entrypoint: the caller outside this file registers the exported handler for GET /rest/saveLoginIp; the handler receives the attacker-controlled Express request object and authenticates the associated user.
The handler reads the caller-supplied `true-client-ip` header, using its first value when the header is an array.
When `httpHeaderXssChallenge` is enabled, the true branch is empty and the sanitization call in the else branch is skipped, allowing the header value to remain attacker-controlled.

The unsanitized value reaches the persistence sink as the authenticated user's `lastLoginIp` property. A later UI or HTML-rendering path outside this file can render the stored payload and execute it in the application's origin.

title: Unauthenticated disclosure of users' security questions
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/user/security-question handler accepts an arbitrary email address and retrieves the associated user's security answer/question without authenticating the caller or verifying ownership. An attacker can submit another user's email and receive that user's security question; the differing responses (question versus {}) also enable account enumeration. If security questions participate in account recovery, this exposes a prerequisite authentication factor and facilitates targeted recovery attacks.

trace.description: The exported handler is registered for GET /rest/user/security-question without authentication middleware; the route caller is outside this file. The handler receives the request query object here.
The caller-controlled query.email value is converted to a string and used as the target user's identifier, with no authentication, ownership, or authorization check.
The handler performs a SecurityAnswerModel lookup scoped only by the supplied email address, allowing a caller to select another user's security-answer record.

When a matching record exists, the associated security question is returned directly in the unauthenticated response. When it does not exist, an empty object is returned, creating an account-enumeration oracle as well.

title: Caller-controlled MongoDB $where JavaScript enables NoSQL injection and query DoS
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/products/:id/reviews handler incorporates caller-controlled req.params.id into a MongoDB $where JavaScript expression. When the noSqlCommandChallenge is enabled, the value is only truncated to 40 characters; truncation is not validation or escaping. An attacker can supply JavaScript syntax that changes the predicate or performs expensive computation during query evaluation, such as injecting statements/loops into the $where expression. Because $where executes server-side JavaScript, this can expose arbitrary query behavior and consume database CPU, potentially causing denial of service.

The handler reads req.params.id. In the challenge-enabled branch it applies only utils.trunc(..., 40), which limits length but does not constrain the value to a numeric product identifier or escape JavaScript syntax.

The resulting value is concatenated into a MongoDB $where JavaScript expression and executed by find(). The input therefore reaches an interpreter without parameterization or an effective allow-list; injected predicates or computationally expensive JavaScript can alter query behavior or consume database resources.

title: Authenticated users can modify arbitrary product reviews
description: The PATCH /rest/products/reviews handler is authenticated but does not authorize the target review against the authenticated user. It reads the review identifier from req.body.id and updates the matching review without using the user value obtained from security.authenticatedUsers.from(req). Any authenticated user can submit another user's review ID and replace its message, causing unauthorized cross-user modification.

The handler obtains the authenticated user, but the value is never used in the subsequent lookup or update to enforce ownership or another per-review authorization rule.
The request body identifier is used to select a review for update, and the message is persisted without any ownership predicate involving the authenticated user.

title: NoSQL operator injection enables bulk review tampering
description: The MongoDB selector embeds req.body.id directly as a query value and accepts attacker-controlled JSON object values. An attacker can supply an operator-shaped identifier such as {"$ne":null}, producing a selector equivalent to {_id: {$ne: null}}. Because the update uses multi: true, this can match and overwrite many or all reviews with the attacker-controlled message. This is NoSQL query injection with broad data-integrity impact.

The unvalidated req.body.id value is placed directly into the MongoDB filter. No scalar type check or allow-list prevents an object containing MongoDB query operators.
The attacker-controlled filter is passed to reviewsCollection.update with multi: true, allowing an injected selector to update multiple matching reviews and persist the attacker-controlled message.

title: Caller-controlled input interpolated into MongoDB $where JavaScript
description: The unauthenticated GET /rest/track-order/:id handler incorporates the caller-controlled path parameter into a MongoDB $where JavaScript expression. When the reflectedXssChallenge is enabled, line 15 only truncates the value and does not escape quotes or other JavaScript syntax. An attacker can supply a value such as `x' || true || '` to alter the expression generated at line 17, potentially causing the query to match arbitrary orders or otherwise execute attacker-controlled query logic. The normal branch removes non-word characters, but that control is conditional and is bypassed whenever the challenge is enabled.

The handler reads req.params.id. If reflectedXssChallenge is enabled, it applies only truncation, leaving quote characters and JavaScript syntax intact.
The resulting value is interpolated directly into a MongoDB $where string, where it is interpreted as JavaScript rather than treated as a bound scalar value.

title: Unauthenticated order lookup lacks object-level authorization
description: The route is registered without authentication or authorization middleware and uses the caller-supplied order identifier to retrieve an order. The MongoDB lookup is scoped only by `orderId`; it does not constrain the record to the authenticated user or another authorization context. The resulting record is returned directly as JSON. Anyone who obtains or guesses another customer's order ID can therefore access that customer's order-tracking data, constituting broken object-level authorization.

trace.description: The caller is outside this file; this handler is exposed as GET /rest/track-order/:id with no authentication middleware, and receives the target order identifier through req.params.id.
The supplied identifier is normalized and then used as the sole lookup key; no authenticated user identity or ownership constraint is introduced.
The database query searches orders by orderId alone, without a per-user ownership or access check.
The first matching order is serialized and returned to the requester as JSON.

title: Unsanitized username enables stored XSS
description: The profile update accepts `req.body.username` and persists it directly without sanitization or an explicit safe-character allow-list. A username is typically displayed as user-controlled profile text; if a downstream HTML view renders it unsafely, an attacker can store markup or script that executes in other users' browsers. The persistence point is in this file; the eventual rendering sink is outside the file.

trace.description: The exported handler receives the attacker-controlled HTTP request body; the route caller and POST /profile registration are outside this file.
The handler reads the caller-controlled `req.body.username` value without visible validation, encoding, or an allow-list.
The unchecked username is persisted through `user.update`, creating a stored attacker-controlled profile value that can execute when rendered by a downstream client or HTML view outside this file.

title: Authentication token cookie lacks security attributes
description: After authenticating a request using the token map, the handler issues a new authentication token and places it in a cookie without setting `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, or `SameSite` attributes. Consequently, the token can be exposed to same-origin script (if an XSS exists), transmitted over an unencrypted HTTP connection, and may be sent in cross-site requests. The absence of a cookie security policy is visible at the token-setting sink, although global middleware could partially mitigate some attributes.

trace.description: The exported POST /profile handler receives an authenticated request from outside this file and uses the request cookie token to identify the session.
After updating the profile, the handler generates and stores a replacement authentication token for the user.
The replacement authentication token is sent in a cookie with no `httpOnly`, `secure`, or `sameSite` options, leaving session protection dependent on controls not shown here.

title: Cookie-authenticated profile mutation lacks CSRF protection
description: This state-changing endpoint authenticates solely with a cookie but contains no visible CSRF-token or Origin/Referer validation. Because the route is registered without middleware and performs a username mutation, a cross-site request can potentially cause a logged-in victim's browser to update the profile. The exploitability depends partly on browser cookie SameSite defaults and deployment configuration, but this handler itself does not enforce the required cross-site request control.

The only request identity check is lookup of `req.cookies.token`; there is no CSRF token, Origin check, or equivalent proof that the mutation originated from the user's application.
The handler mutates the authenticated user's profile based on the request body and redirects normally, so a forged cross-site POST can perform the state change when the session cookie is sent.

title: User-controlled username reaches server-side eval
description: The authenticated user's username is treated as executable JavaScript. The username is read from the database and, when it matches the `#{...}` pattern and the challenge is enabled, the contents are passed directly to `eval()` without validation or sandboxing. An attacker who can create or modify a username can supply JavaScript that executes in the server process, potentially reading secrets, modifying application state, or executing arbitrary server-side actions.

trace.description: The exported profile handler receives the HTTP request; its caller and route registration are outside this file. The handler processes the unauthenticated route declaration's request and obtains the authentication token from the request cookies.
The handler resolves the logged-in user's identity from the request cookie and loads that user's database record.

The username is copied from the user record and checked for the special `#{...}` syntax. This value originates from user-controlled account data, although the username creation/update path is outside this file.
The extracted username contents are passed directly to `eval()` when the challenge is enabled. There is no allow-list, sandbox, or other restriction on the JavaScript expression.

title: Stored username injection into dynamically compiled Pug template
description: The handler performs textual substitution of the database-backed username directly into the Pug source and then compiles the resulting string as a server-side template. The username is not safely encoded for the Pug language; the attempted leading backslash does not safely constrain multiline or template syntax injected into the replacement. A crafted username can therefore alter the generated Pug source and execute template expressions or statements during compilation/rendering, causing server-side code execution or unauthorized data exposure.

trace.description: The exported profile handler receives the HTTP request; its caller and route registration are outside this file.
The handler loads the current user's record from the authenticated cookie identity.
The username is taken from the user record. The account-data mutation path is outside this file, but the value is attacker-influenced if a user can choose or modify their username.
The username is inserted into the Pug source with string replacement rather than being passed as data to a fixed template or encoded for Pug syntax.
The modified string is compiled as executable Pug template source and rendered. Any injected Pug/template syntax is interpreted by the server.

title: Unescaped promotion subtitles enable stored XSS in the promotion page
description: The public promotion page embeds the contents of a configured subtitle file directly into an HTML response inside a script element without HTML/script-context escaping. If an attacker can influence the subtitle file (or deployment configuration causes it to reference attacker-controlled content), a payload containing `</script><script>...</script>` can terminate the inert VTT script element and execute JavaScript when a user visits `/promotion`. The caller and any mechanism that controls the subtitle file are outside this file, so exploitability depends on that external control path.

trace.description: The exported `promotionVideo` handler is registered for unauthenticated `GET /promotion`; the route caller is outside this file.

The handler reads the subtitle filename from configuration and loads the corresponding file from the application video directory. The subtitle file is treated as trusted text, with no size or content validation shown here.
The subtitle file contents are returned verbatim to the caller of `getSubsFromFile`, without HTML or script-context escaping.

The raw subtitle contents are concatenated into a `<script type="text/vtt">` element and the resulting HTML is sent to the browser. A `</script>` sequence in the subtitle data can escape the element and inject executable markup/script.

title: CAPTCHA verification is bypassed unconditionally
description: The CAPTCHA challenge middleware does not validate a CAPTCHA response or otherwise authenticate the caller. Instead, every unauthenticated request records a current timestamp as if it had satisfied the CAPTCHA and then unconditionally calls next(). An attacker can therefore automate requests to the protected Feedbacks route without solving the CAPTCHA, enabling spam and other abuse of the downstream handler.

The middleware writes the current time into the application's CAPTCHA-bypass tracking state without examining any request-supplied CAPTCHA answer or other proof of challenge completion.
The middleware unconditionally forwards the request to the downstream Feedbacks handler, so the route can be reached after only this ineffective challenge step.

title: Unauthenticated CAPTCHA bypass state grows without bound
description: Each unauthenticated request to the CAPTCHA-bypass middleware writes to an index derived from a monotonically increasing global counter. Because the counter is incremented for every request and there is no bound, expiry, cleanup, or rate limit in this code, repeated requests can grow captchaBypassReqTimes indefinitely and consume process memory. title: Hardcoded password and TOTP seed for an existing account
